topic: Advent of Europeans in Indian History
description: Following the discovery of new sea routes in the 15th century, European powers arrived in India primarily for trade. The major European entities—Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danes, and French—started as trading companies but eventually engaged in fierce rivalries, culminating in British political supremacy over India.

sections.title: Arrival of the Portuguese
sections.description: The Portuguese were the first Europeans to discover a direct sea route to India, aiming to monopolize the highly profitable Eastern spice trade.

key_concepts.explanation: A strategy introduced by Francisco de Almeida (the first Portuguese Governor) to establish Portuguese naval dominance in the Indian Ocean rather than expanding territorial empire on land.
A naval trade license or pass issued by the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean. Any ship sailing without this permit was liable to be captured or sunk by the Portuguese armada.

historical_events.significance: Vasco da Gama reached the port of Calicut on the western coast of India via the Cape of Good Hope, welcomed by the local ruler Zamorin.
Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur, Yusuf Adil Shah. Goa later became the capital of the Portuguese Indian Empire.

key_associations.associated_with: Real Founder of Portuguese Power in India
key_associations.extra_info: He captured Goa, abolished the practice of Sati in his territories, and encouraged his men to marry local Indian women to build a permanent settlement.

important_facts.fact: The Portuguese were the first Europeans to arrive in India (1498) and the last to leave, vacating Goa only in 1961 after 'Operation Vijay' by the Indian Armed Forces.
They introduced tobacco cultivation, cashew nuts, pineapples, and the printing press (first press set up in Goa in 1556) to India.

sections.title: The Dutch East India Company
sections.description: The Dutch (people from the Netherlands/Holland) formed a powerful joint-stock company but focused more on the Indonesian archipelago (Spice Islands) than on India.

historical_events.significance: The Dutch government amalgamated several trading companies into a single United East India Company, granting it a monopoly over Asian trade.
The Dutch established their first Indian trading factory at Masulipatnam in Andhra Pradesh.
The British forces decisively defeated the Dutch, ending Dutch political and commercial ambitions in India.

important_facts.fact: Unlike the Portuguese, the Dutch focused on the export of Indian cotton textiles rather than spices, making textiles the primary export commodity from India.
Pulicat was the main center of the Dutch in India, where they minted gold coins known as 'Pagodas'.

sections.title: Arrival and Expansion of the English
sections.description: The British East India Company gradually transformed from a mere trading body into the paramount political power in the Indian subcontinent.

key_concepts.explanation: A royal decree (Farman) issued by Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar granting the British East India Company duty-free trading rights in Bengal, Gujarat, and the Deccan.

historical_events.significance: Queen Elizabeth I granted a royal charter to the 'Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies', giving them a 15-year monopoly.
After Captain Thomas Best defeated the Portuguese at Swally, Mughal Emperor Jahangir permitted the British to establish a permanent factory at Surat.
Sent as an ambassador by King James I to Jahangir's court, he succeeded in securing privileges to set up factories in various parts of the Mughal Empire.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: Founded by Job Charnock by amalgamating three villages: Sutanuti, Gobindpur, and Kalikata. It became the seat of British power in India.
Constructed in 1639 after Francis Day acquired the lease of Madras from the ruler of Chandragiri. It was the first British fortress in India.

sections.title: The French East India Company
sections.description: The French were the last major European power to enter the Indian trade market. Their state-controlled company fiercely competed with the British for supremacy.

key_concepts.explanation: A series of three military conflicts between the British and the French in the Carnatic region (South India) for trade monopoly and political control.

historical_events.event: Formation of Compagnie des Indes Orientales
historical_events.significance: Established under the patronage of King Louis XIV's finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was heavily dependent on the French government.
Francois Caron established the first French trading factory in India at Surat.
Fought during the Third Carnatic War. The British forces under Sir Eyre Coote decisively defeated the French under Comte de Lally, effectively ending the French empire in India.

key_associations.extra_info: He was the first European to intervene in internal Indian disputes to acquire political territories and originated the concept of the 'Subsidiary Alliance' (later perfected by Lord Wellesley).

sections.title: The Danes and Chronology of European Arrival
sections.description: Important chronological sequences frequently asked in exams, along with a brief overview of the Danish East India Company.

key_associations.extra_info: Mnemonic: P-D-E-D-F. Remember that the Dutch arrived before the English.
Note: The English East India Company was formed before the Dutch East India Company, despite the Dutch physically arriving in India first.

important_facts.fact: The Danish East India Company was formed in 1616. Their principal settlements in India were Tranquebar (Tamil Nadu) and Serampore (Bengal), which was their headquarters.
The Danes failed to strengthen their position in India and ultimately sold all their Indian settlements to the British Government in 1845.
